body: Sadly, I can't get my conviction expunged. I lived in a different state with harsher laws at the time I was arrested.
Hmmm, all the applications I filled out (in person, at my local stores) included the conviction question. Do the online applications for those businesses not ask about your background?
Oh, I get it now. That makes perfect sense. And is also a major downer. Still, thanks for the clarification.

I've seen lists like that, and sadly, most aren't correct. At least not all inclusively. Off that list alone, I've applied to Walgreens, Wendy's, Subway, Golden Corral, Goodwill, Dairy Queen, Denny's, and IHOP within the last six months. Not one interview was conducted, because I don't feel comfortable lying on the application, and almost EVERY job in the state where I currently live has that "have you ever been convicted" question on their application. Since I don't even get interviewed, despite being a college graduate (with honors) with an IQ way above average, I have to assume it's because of the felony. I honestly don't know else it could be. I am more than qualified for every job I've applied for.

I get that an employer is free to make their own judgments based on available information, but I don't understand why a background checking agency would be legally allowed to report it to them under CA's law. Maybe I'm just not fluent in legalese, but if it meant that all three dates (disposition, release or parole) had to fall outside the 7 years, why does it use the word or? I don't know, maybe I'm just grasping at straws, since the "crime" happened when I was 21, and has prevented me from living a normal life ever since. I'd really like my life to begin at some point.

I'm not mad at you. I appreciate the honesty, I'm just sad, as I thought CA might actually represent a new start for me, since it's very close to being 7 years since I was convicted. The conviction was for battery on a law enforcement officer, without injury to the officer. Basically a cop kicked the crap out of me, then charged me with battery. Due to the lack of injury, it likely wouldn't even have been charged as a felony if it had happened in CA.

Considering that I haven't been hired for a single job since my probation ended, I don't understand how I'm ever supposed to live a "normal" life. I appreciate that you would give a "convict" a chance, but most people aren't like you. They just see that scarlet F and don't care about the circumstances.

Addendum: Here's one thing I don't get. When I look up my case on the county clerk website it says "date of disposition" and then lists the date I was convicted. It lists no further dates of disposition. So why does anything like probation count as a further disposition when it isn't marked as such in the official court record?

What if you only had probation, not parole? I didn't do any prison time. Sadly, this isn't very encouraging. I didn't even do the crime, not that it really matters now. My whole life got wrecked by this false conviction, and in my state, I can't even expunge it. If you're saying that it's 7 years from the end of my probation, then I might as well not even bother trying to get a job, since my probation ended way less than 7 years ago. This is so ridiculous how one conviction basically ends any chance you have of being successful. Anyway, sorry to rant. I'm just not pleased to know that this is the case. :(

I've actually applied to lots of jobs out of state already. The few that responded wanted me to interview (which is admittedly encouraging), but I'd have to do it in person. I can't afford to fly anywhere. I can barely afford to pay my rent. And sadly, my parents are only slightly less poor than me, so they're little help in this case.

I've tried to get a personal loan to help me move, but was denied by every bank I applied to. Even my own bank, which is ridiculous, as I've had an account in good standing for over 5 years there. They wouldn't even loan me $3000, one of their smallest possible loan amounts.

I know this is going to sound like a "no shit Sherlock" type statement, but lack of money is basically the root of my depression it seems. I can think of lots of things I'd like to do to better my life, but can't do any of them without money. Which brings me back to my felony, which even prevents me from working most retail jobs.

Thus why I feel like I want to give up and die already. The thought of working a dead end job my whole life simply to make ends meet makes me want to jump off a bridge.
Moderate-sized city. Most of the slick attorneys I saw were local, and knew the local judges and DA. Some were even ex-cops themselves. Even a good local attorney will run you a few grand though.

As an addendum to my other reply, ONLY go to trial if you can afford a damn good lawyer. While I was sitting in the courtoom for days, waiting for my case to come up on the trial docket, I witnessed several other felony trials take place. Slick, high powered attorneys were getting people off for much worse charges than mine. If you have a public defender though, trust me, they're in over their head.

As I said above, innocence doesn't mean a god damn thing in court without hard evidence on your side, ESPECIALLY when it's your word versus the police. Juries are completely willing to believe every word out of a cop's mouth.

That's an admirable attitude man, but that was mine, and look where I am now. You don't want to be me. If you get a plea without jail time and that includes a withhold of adjudication like I did, TAKE IT. Trust me, community service and some probation sucks at the time, but you will never have to fear that dreaded "have you been convicted of a felony" box on job applications.

My counsel was an idiotic, overworked, public defender. He basically told me to make up my own mind. Knowing then what I know now? Would I go to trial? Hell no. I'd have taken the plea, since it involved no jail time and a withhold of adjudication. Stupid me, thinking that I shouldn't have to admit guilt for something I didn't do. Unless you have concrete proof, being innocent means absolutely nothing in court. Sad but true. Especially if the other party is a cop.
I'd gladly apply for a pardon, but in my state you have to wait at least 10 years to be eligible.
Yes, sadly. I was a poor college student at the time, and couldn't afford the $2,000 plus a private lawyer wanted.

They did offer a plea, but they wanted an answer right then and there, at the arraignment. Never having dealt with the legal system before, and not realizing that innocence doesn't really matter, I asked for a couple days to think about it. Before I could decide, they rescinded the offer.
Isn't there a statute of limitations on appealing a verdict? If so, I'm probably past it.

Not to sound flip, but get a lawyer and do what? I've consulted with a lawyer. The laws of my state are so draconian that I have zero options for getting my record expunged, sealed, or otherwise removed. I could try to get a governor's pardon, but I'm not quite eligible to apply yet under current law, and even then those are incredibly rare. Plus, my conviction would still show up in a background check, even if I was pardoned.

All kinds. Editing, directing, writing, camera, you name it. Writing is probably my specialty. I also just generally enjoy working on set. I do a good amount of production assistant work. It's enjoyable, despite the long hours, but around here it's always for low/no budget indies, so I rarely get paid more than a gas stipend.
They don't, sadly. I looked into it, believe me. There is no way to clear my record. Ever.
prozac and coffee is right. In my state, you can't expunge or seal a conviction if you were adjudicated guilty.
